nodes.name: Tabetheus
nodes.role: Roman Egyptian woman and papyrus letter writer
nodes.location: Alexandria or the Karanis network, Egypt
nodes.bio: Tabetheus was a Roman Egyptian woman whose Greek letters to her brother Claudius Tiberianus survive as P.Mich. VIII 473 and, probably, P.Mich. VIII 474. Her letters show family correspondence in the Tiberianus archive: linen, money, rations, children, illness, travel to Alexandria, and the urgent wish that Tiberianus visit after a long absence.

nodes.name: Palladius, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Learned bearer and correspondent in Procopius of Gaza's circle
nodes.bio: Palladius is called learned by Procopius of Gaza and carries a letter from Musaeus. Procopius says the sight of Palladius with that letter was more welcome than Croesus's gold.

nodes.name: Ilasius, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Ilasius appears in Procopius of Gaza, Epistles 33, 34, and 74. Procopius links him with practical assistance and, in Epistle 74, teases him about a fruit-bearing place that is less kind to human bodies.

nodes.name: Thomas, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Official, judge, or rhetorically trained correspondent
nodes.bio: Thomas is addressed by Procopius of Gaza in Epistles 42 and 68. Procopius first praises him as a just and eloquent official, then writes of memory and longing as a substitute for the sight of good men.

nodes.name: Ulpius, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Ulpius is addressed by Procopius of Gaza in Epistles 49 and 51. Strategius's affairs reopen the exchange between them, and Procopius turns delayed letters into a mock indictment and reconciliation.

nodes.name: Sabinus, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Friend, recipient of a recommendation, and comic target
nodes.bio: Sabinus is a correspondent in Procopius of Gaza's circle. In Epistle 131, Procopius turns Sabinus's reproach about poverty into a sharp comic sermon on money, rhetoric, public display, and the goddess Poverty.

nodes.name: Cyriacus, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Correspondent addressed about gifts and parents
nodes.bio: Cyriacus is addressed by Procopius of Gaza in two short letters: one comic note about food gifts and one serious exhortation about the gratitude children owe their parents.

nodes.name: Musaeus, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Literary correspondent and sender of Palladius
nodes.bio: Musaeus receives Procopius's thanks for books and later sends a letter by Palladius. Procopius treats him as a friend whose contact with books and messengers can make them dearer.

nodes.name: Marcellinus, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Marcellinus was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 31. Chrysostom renews an old friendship with Marcellinus after mutual silence.

nodes.name: Euthalia, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Euthalia was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 32. Chrysostom praises Euthalia's spiritual steadiness and asks for letters about her security and health.

nodes.name: Tranquillinus, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Tranquillinus was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 37. Chrysostom sends the ill bishop Seleucus to Tranquillinus and asks for news that Eutychius failed to bring.

nodes.name: Hymnetius, chief physician and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Hymnetius was a chief physician addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 38. Chrysostom entrusts the coughing bishop Seleucus to Hymnetius's medical skill.

nodes.name: Asyncritia, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Asyncritia was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 40. Chrysostom consoles Asyncritia in affliction and asks whether her illness has eased.

nodes.name: Arabius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Arabius was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 48. Chrysostom praises Arabius's enduring love and asks for more letters about his health.

nodes.name: Nicolaus, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Nicolaus was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 53. Chrysostom praises Nicolaus's care for Phoenicia and asks him to send Gerontius, John, and other helpers.

nodes.name: Cyriacus, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Cyriacus was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 64. Chrysostom asks Cyriacus to help the son of Sopater, governor of Armenia.

nodes.name: Theodotus, lector and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Theodotus was a lector addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 102. Chrysostom encourages Theodotus to rejoice in trials while caring for his weak eyes.

nodes.name: Asyncritia and her companions, correspondents of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Asyncritia and her companions was a correspondents addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 106. Chrysostom urges Asyncritia and her companions to endure trials for the heavenly prize.

nodes.name: Theodora, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Theodora was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 117. Chrysostom asks Theodora to forgive Eustathius and receive spiritual profit from mercy.

nodes.name: Gemellus, official and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Gemellus was an imperial official addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 124 and 132. Chrysostom praises his public authority, concern for justice, and desire for Christian initiation.

nodes.name: Polybius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Polybius was a correspondent of John Chrysostom addressed in PG 52 Epistulae 127 and 143. Chrysostom writes to him about dangerous exile conditions and the way friendship overcomes physical separation.

nodes.name: Hypatius, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Hypatius was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 180. Chrysostom blesses Hypatius for endurance in persecution and asks for news of his health.

nodes.name: Hesychius, bishop of Salona
nodes.bio: Hesychius of Salona was a Dalmatian bishop who corresponded with Augustine about interpreting the signs of the end of the age. He also appears in late antique episcopal correspondence addressed from the eastern Mediterranean.

nodes.name: Brison, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Brison was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 190. Chrysostom gently rebukes Brison for failing to write despite publicly showing affection.

nodes.name: Diodorus the Scholasticus
nodes.bio: Diodorus the Scholasticus is addressed in Aeneas of Gaza, Letters 7 and 22, both witty notes about reconciliation, friendship, speech, and silence.

nodes.name: Epiphanius, sophist and correspondent of Aeneas of Gaza
nodes.bio: Epiphanius the Sophist receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letters 12 and 23, one about Aeneas's portrait and one recommending a well-educated traveler.

nodes.name: Celer of Hippo
nodes.role: North African landowner and Augustine correspondent
nodes.bio: Celer was a wealthy landowner in the Hippo region whom Augustine pressed toward serious Christian study and away from Donatist allegiance.

nodes.name: Macedonius, imperial official and correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Macedonius was a secular official who corresponded with Augustine about legal intercession and admired Augustine's early books of the City of God.

nodes.name: Valerius, count of Africa
nodes.bio: Valerius was a high Roman official in Africa whom Augustine addressed as an influential Christian patron able to help bishops and churches.

nodes.name: Aurelius, Silvanus, and Catholic bishops
nodes.bio: Aurelius, Silvanus, and the Catholic bishops were North African episcopal signatories who accepted Marcellinus's terms for the 411 conference with Donatist bishops at Carthage.

nodes.name: Marcellinus
nodes.bio: Marcellinus was a Roman tribune and imperial notary who presided over the 411 Carthage conference between Catholic and Donatist bishops and corresponded with Augustine.

nodes.name: Aurelius and Carthage council bishops
nodes.bio: Aurelius of Carthage and the bishops gathered at Carthage represented the North African episcopate in the Pelagian controversy. Their appeal to Innocent I asked Rome to confirm African judgments on grace, free choice, and infant baptism.

nodes.name: Nicias, bishop and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Bishop and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Nicias was a bishop addressed by Severus of Antioch in a letter about irregular ordinations connected with Minidus and Uaris. His secure see is not identified in the Brooks heading, so he is kept as an ungeolocated ecclesiastical correspondent until a stronger source is found.

nodes.name: Entrechius, bishop of Anazarbus
nodes.role: Bishop of Anazarbus and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Entrechius was bishop of Anazarbus and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. Severus writes to him about the church of Rhosus and the proper election procedure for choosing a bishop.

nodes.name: Cassian, bishop of Bostra
nodes.role: Bishop of Bostra and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Cassian was bishop of Bostra and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. Several letters address problems in his circle, including irregular episcopal acts, discipline of Agapius, and the canonical status of a man who had been castrated by physicians.

nodes.name: Theotecnus, archiatros and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Chief physician and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Theotecnus was an archiatros, or chief physician, addressed by Severus of Antioch. Severus' letter reports ecclesiastical news from the royal city, including debates over the council at Chalcedon and the commemoration of Nestorius at Tarsus.

nodes.name: Monks of the monastery of Isaac addressed by Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Monastic correspondents of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: These monks of the monastery of Isaac were addressed by Severus of Antioch after the affair of Antipater and during the episcopal election for Anasartha. Severus presses them to accept Stephen for the common benefit of the churches.

nodes.name: Andrew, reader and notary
nodes.role: Reader, notary, and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Andrew was a reader and notary addressed by Severus of Antioch during exile. His letter to Severus arrived with one from expelled virgins of Antioch, and Severus answers questions about prayer at martyr shrines and the death of Zosimus.

nodes.name: Suffragan bishops under Apamea addressed by Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Bishops under the metropolitan see of Apamea and correspondents of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: These suffragan bishops belonged to the ecclesiastical province under Apamea. Severus addressed them about their separation from Peter of Apamea and later summoned them to a regular synod for the common peace of the churches.

nodes.name: Didymus, bishop and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Bishop and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Didymus was a bishop addressed by Severus of Antioch about the restoration of the deacon Sannus. The letter shows Severus applying gradual pastoral correction rather than abandoning a repentant cleric after one fault.

nodes.name: Orthodox clergy and laity of Antioch addressed by Severus
nodes.role: Clergy and lay believers of Antioch addressed by Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: These clergy and lay believers formed the church community in Antioch to which Severus wrote during exile. He encourages them to endure suffering, preserve the faith, and avoid communion that would compromise their confession.

nodes.name: Misael the chamberlain
nodes.role: Chamberlain and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Misael was a chamberlain addressed by Severus about debts, ordinations, and the financial distress of the church of Antioch after Severus became bishop.

nodes.name: Simeon, bishop of Chalcis
nodes.role: Bishop of Chalcis and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Simeon was bishop of Chalcis, the Syrian city also known as Qenneshrin, and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. The letters preserved as I.37 and I.38 show Severus urging him to resolve disciplinary trouble involving monks, clergy, and canonical inhibitions with both firmness and respect for Simeon's age and authority.

nodes.name: Misael the deacon
nodes.role: Deacon and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Misael the deacon corresponded with Severus about communion, gifts, and the validity of sacraments performed by orthodox clergy whose personal character might differ.

nodes.name: Unknown monk, correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus
nodes.bio: This unnamed monastic correspondent is identified only by the recipient label in the Evagrius CPG 2437 parallel edition. Further identification and geolocation require specialist review.

nodes.name: Abba Lucian, correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus
nodes.bio: Abba Lucian is named as recipient of Evagrius Ponticus, Letter 4, in the CPG 2437 parallel edition. The letter asks him to review and correct Evagrius's Antirrhetikos material on demonic thoughts.

nodes.name: Unknown monastic elder, correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus
nodes.bio: Unknown monastic elder, correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus is the working identity for Letters 52 and 53 in the Evagrius CPG 2437 parallel tradition. The source preserves the correspondence context but not enough evidence for a secure personal identity or destination geolocation.

nodes.name: Unknown recipient of Severus of Antioch I.61-I.62
nodes.role: Unidentified correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: The recipient of Select Letters I.61-I.62 is not preserved in Brooks' table of contents: I.61 is marked as having lost its heading, and I.62 is marked as addressed to the same person. The surviving letters concern accusations, discipline, bishops, deaconesses, and the proper evidentiary standard for ecclesiastical judgment.

nodes.name: Mardonius, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Mardonius is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 845, dated 388. The letter thanks him for friendly support and defends Libanius' loyalty to the emperor during a political crisis. His secure location is not stated in the letter heading.

nodes.name: Saturninus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Saturninus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 857, dated 388. Libanius commends Diognetus to his judgment and asks him to help a rhetor silenced by a legal restriction. Exact office and location remain uncertain from this heading alone.

nodes.name: Panhellenius, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.role: literary and civic correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Panhellenius is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistles 861 and 863, dated 388. Libanius commends Domnion to him and later rebukes him affectionately for leaving Antioch during the display season.

nodes.name: Celsinus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.role: literary and civic correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Celsinus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 877, dated 388. The letter connects him with Letoius, Beirut, hospitality, literary performance, marriage, and hoped-for visits to Antioch.

nodes.name: Africanus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.role: legal and patronage correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Africanus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 882, dated 388. The letter asks him to help Petrus recover property and to write on the matter to Egypt.

nodes.name: Sophronius, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Sophronius is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 883, dated 388. Libanius describes him as vital to Constantinople and seeks continued favor for Iasius and Iphicrates.

nodes.name: Leontius, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.role: student and literary correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Leontius is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 894, dated 388. Libanius celebrates a speech whose style so closely resembled his own that listeners suspected the student had mastered the teacher's voice.

nodes.name: Philagrius, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Philagrius is addressed by Libanius in Foerster volume 11. The project keeps the scaffold conservative pending secure external identification.

nodes.name: Ablabius, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Ablabius is addressed by Libanius in Foerster volume 11. The project keeps the scaffold conservative pending secure external identification.

nodes.name: Priscion, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Priscion is addressed by Libanius in Foerster volume 11. The project keeps the scaffold conservative pending secure external identification.

nodes.name: Aburgius, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Aburgius is addressed by Libanius in Foerster volume 11. The project keeps the scaffold conservative pending secure external identification.

nodes.name: Clemens, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Clemens is addressed by Libanius in Foerster volume 11. The project keeps the scaffold conservative pending secure external identification.

nodes.name: Anysius, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Anysius is addressed by Libanius in Foerster volume 11. The project keeps the scaffold conservative pending secure external identification.

nodes.name: Parthenopaeus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Parthenopaeus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster volume 11. The project keeps the scaffold conservative pending secure external identification.

nodes.name: Zenodotus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Zenodotus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster volume 11. The project keeps the scaffold conservative pending secure external identification.

Emperor Theodosius I (correspondent of Isidore of Pelusium)
Ausonius Corrector (correspondent of Isidore of Pelusium)

Paulus, of Naples (correspondent of Isidore of Pelusium)
Antoninus
nodes.bio:
Antoninus (fl. 400s–410s) was a bishop in North Africa and one of Augustine's correspondents on matters of church discipline and pastoral practice. He appears 9 times in this collection as a recipient of Augustine's letters.

Augustine's letters to Antoninus deal with the practical challenges of running a North African diocese in the early fifth century — managing clerical disputes, handling questions of church discipline, and navigating the complex ecclesiastical politics of a region divided by the Donatist schism. They offer a ground-level view of the administrative work that consumed most of a bishop's time.

Antoninus is significant as a representative of the ordinary bishops who formed the backbone of the African church — men whose names history barely remembers but who did the daily work of keeping a complex institution running in difficult times.

Rogatianus Presbyter, and Other Confessors. A.D. 250

Andrew, Monk of Constantinople
nodes.role: monk; correspondent of Theodoret of Cyrrhus and Isidore of Pelusium
nodes.bio: Andrew is named as the recipient of several letters within the fifth-century correspondence of Theodoret of Cyrrhus and Isidore of Pelusium, but he is otherwise little attested and cannot be securely identified with any prominent figure of the period. He is known chiefly as a monk addressed by these correspondents, which places him in the eastern Roman monastic and theological milieu of the first half of the fifth century, very likely in or around Constantinople and the dioceses of Syria and Egypt where Theodoret and Isidore were active. No reliable dates, offices, or biographical events are recorded for him beyond his appearance as a correspondent, so any fuller portrait would be speculative.

nodes.name: People of Lucristanum, Settled on Sontius (Isonzo River)
Triwila, Saio, and Ferrocinctus, Imperial Agent
Barbarians and Romans Residing in Pannonia

Notables, Landowners, Defenders of Syracuse, and Provincials

Vitalianus, Chancellor of Lucania and Bruttium

Dorotheus
nodes.role: correspondent (likely a cleric or official of the Greek East)
nodes.bio: Dorotheus (Greek Dorotheos) is a name attested here only as the recipient of four letters, appearing across the correspondence of Pope Hormisdas of Rome (r. 514-523) and the vast letter collection of Isidore of Pelusium in Egypt (early 5th century). The name was extremely common in late antiquity, and the figure or figures so designated cannot be securely identified or dated from these letters alone; the two collections may well point to two different men of the same name. He is best described as an obscure correspondent, likely a clergyman or lay official of the Greek East, known chiefly through the letters addressed to him rather than from any independent record. No specific dates, offices, or biographical details should be inferred with confidence.

nodes.name: Nilus
nodes.role: correspondent in the circle of Isidore of Pelusium (probable monk or cleric)
nodes.bio: A correspondent named Nilus appears as the recipient of letters in the corpus, associated with the circle of Isidore of Pelusium, the early-fifth-century priest and prolific letter-writer of the eastern Nile Delta. Several monks and clergy named Nilus circulated in the ascetic and ecclesiastical networks of late-antique Egypt and Asia Minor, and the figure here is most plausibly such a monastic or clerical associate to whom these letters of spiritual and exegetical counsel were addressed. He is not independently well documented: beyond his appearance as an addressee in this correspondence, little can be said with confidence about his offices, dates, or biography without conflating him with the better-known ascetic writer Nilus of Ancyra, an identification the evidence here does not establish.

nodes.name: Hermogenes
nodes.role: correspondent of Julian and of Isidore of Pelusium (likely a high imperial official in the Julian letter)
nodes.bio: Hermogenes is a common Greek name attached here to correspondents in two distinct collections, the letters of the emperor Julian (r. 361-363) and those of Isidore of Pelusium (d. c. 450), so these records may not all refer to the same man. Julian addressed a letter to a Hermogenes who had served as a high imperial official (often identified with the Hermogenes who was prefect of Egypt under Constantius II, later honored by Julian); the Hermogenes in Isidore's correspondence is a separate, otherwise little-known figure in early-fifth-century Egypt. Beyond what these letters reveal, the individual(s) are not richly documented, and specific dates, offices, and biography cannot be securely fixed without conflating different people.

nodes.name: Agathodaimon
nodes.bio: Agathodaimon is known only as the recipient of four short letters from Isidore of Pelusium (c. 360-c. 435 AD), the ascetic and biblical commentator whose vast correspondence touches hundreds of named addressees across late-antique Egypt. Nothing certain is recorded of his life, office, or dates beyond this epistolary attestation; the Greek name ("good spirit/fortune") was common in Egypt and gives no further identification. Based on Isidore's milieu, he was most plausibly a cleric, monk, or local correspondent active in the Pelusium region of the Nile Delta in the early fifth century, but this is an inference from context rather than independently documented fact.

nodes.name: Paulos
nodes.role: correspondent of Libanius and Isidore of Pelusium
nodes.bio: Otherwise little attested; known chiefly as the recipient of letters under the very common name Paulus/Paulos (Greek Παῦλος). The nine letters addressed to a "Paulos" in this corpus span two quite different milieus -- the school of the pagan rhetorician Libanius at Antioch (later 4th century) and the ascetic correspondence of Isidore of Pelusium in Egypt (early-to-mid 5th century) -- so the name almost certainly stands for more than one individual rather than a single traceable person. In Libanius's letters a Paulus typically figures as a former student, official, or local notable; in Isidore's, a Paulus is generally a cleric, monk, or layman receiving moral and exegetical instruction. No specific dates, offices, or biography can be assigned with confidence beyond what the letters themselves imply.

nodes.name: Dorotheos, bishop
nodes.bio: A bishop named Dorotheos addressed as a recipient of letters within the corpus (Greek address Δωροθέῳ ἐπισκόπῳ, 'to Dorotheos the bishop'). He is otherwise little attested and is known chiefly as a correspondent, with no secure independent biographical record. The episcopal title and the association with the letters of Isidore of Pelusium place him most plausibly in the early-fifth-century Christian milieu of Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean, where Isidore corresponded with numerous bishops, clergy, and officials on matters of scripture, doctrine, and church discipline. Dorotheos was a very common Greek name and several bishops bore it in this period, so this figure should not be confidently identified with any of the better-known holders of the name; what is genuinely known is limited to his appearance as an addressee.

nodes.name: Athanasios
nodes.role: correspondent of Libanius and Isidore of Pelusium
nodes.bio: A correspondent named Athanasius (Greek Athanasios), known here chiefly as the recipient of thirteen letters within the collections of Libanius and Isidore of Pelusium. The name was extremely common in the Greek-speaking late-antique world, and these letters do not clearly correspond to any single famous bearer; the recipient is far more likely one (or several) of the minor officials, rhetors, students, or ecclesiastics with whom Libanius (the pagan rhetor of Antioch, c. 314-393) and Isidore of Pelusium (Christian ascetic and letter-writer in Egypt, c. 360-435) regularly exchanged correspondence. He should NOT be conflated with the celebrated Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria; no evidence in the letters supports that identification. Beyond his appearance as an addressee, little can be said with confidence about his career or biography.

Neidos
nodes.bio: Otherwise little attested; Neidos is known chiefly as a recipient of five letters from Isidore of Pelusium, the early-fifth-century ascetic and biblical commentator whose vast correspondence (some 2,000 short letters) survives in the Patrologia Graeca. He is addressed as a scholasticus, the late-antique term for a trained advocate or man of legal/rhetorical education, and so was probably a lay professional active in or near Pelusium in the eastern Nile Delta during the first half of the fifth century. Nothing further about his life, career, or dates can be established with confidence beyond what Isidore's letters imply.

nodes.name: Church of Ephesus
nodes.bio: Christian community at Ephesus in Asia Minor, recipient of Ignatius's letter (~110 AD). Bishop Onesimus led the community.

nodes.name: Church of Magnesia
nodes.bio: Christian community at Magnesia near the Maeander in Asia Minor. Bishop Damas led a young but well-ordered community.

nodes.name: Church of Tralles
nodes.bio: Christian community at Tralles in Asia Minor. Bishop Polybius represented them to Ignatius at Smyrna.

nodes.name: Church of Rome
nodes.bio: Christian community at Rome, addressed by Ignatius with special reverence. He implored them not to intervene to prevent his martyrdom.

nodes.name: Church of Philadelphia
nodes.bio: Christian community at Philadelphia in Lydia (Asia Minor), recipient of Ignatius's letter emphasizing unity and the Eucharist.

nodes.name: Church of Smyrna
nodes.bio: Christian community at Smyrna in Asia Minor. Ignatius wrote from Smyrna and also addressed a letter to the community.

nodes.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
nodes.bio: Bishop of Smyrna, disciple of the Apostle John, martyred c. 155. Recipient of Ignatius's personal letter of guidance.

nodes.name: John of Antioch
nodes.bio: Patriarch of Antioch (429-441). Initially supported Nestorius but reconciled with Cyril through the Formula of Reunion (433).

nodes.name: Eusebius, correspondent of Gregory of Nyssa
nodes.bio: Eusebius is the named recipient of Gregory of Nyssa's first letter in the NPNF selection. The public-domain NPNF title does not securely identify him.

nodes.name: City of Sebasteia
nodes.bio: Sebasteia, modern Sivas in central Anatolia, was an important city of Roman Armenia and Cappadocia. Gregory addressed the city in a doctrinal letter preserved in the NPNF selection.

nodes.name: Ablabius, correspondent of Gregory of Nyssa
nodes.bio: Ablabius is the recipient of Gregory of Nyssa's third NPNF letter. The letter preserves Gregory's account of his return journey and reception by his community.

nodes.name: Cynegius, correspondent of Gregory of Nyssa
nodes.bio: Cynegius is the named recipient of Gregory of Nyssa's fourth letter in the NPNF selection. His exact identification is not settled by the public-domain title alone.

nodes.name: Recipient of Gregory of Nyssa's testimonial
nodes.bio: The recipient of Gregory of Nyssa's fifth NPNF letter is not named in the source title; the letter is transmitted as a testimonial.

nodes.name: Stagirius, correspondent of Gregory of Nyssa
nodes.bio: Stagirius is the named recipient of Gregory of Nyssa's sixth letter in the NPNF selection.

nodes.name: Unnamed friend of Gregory of Nyssa
nodes.bio: This unnamed friend is the recipient of Gregory of Nyssa's seventh NPNF letter.

nodes.name: Student of classical literature addressed by Gregory of Nyssa
nodes.bio: Gregory's eighth NPNF letter addresses a young student devoted to classical literature and his father.

nodes.name: Unnamed invitee of Gregory of Nyssa
nodes.bio: The ninth NPNF letter is transmitted as an invitation without a personal recipient named in the title.

nodes.name: Recipient of Gregory of Nyssa's letter on Against Eunomius
nodes.bio: The twelfth NPNF letter concerns Gregory of Nyssa's work against Eunomius; the public-domain title does not name the recipient.

nodes.name: Church at Nicomedia
nodes.bio: The church at Nicomedia, an important city on the Propontis, received Gregory of Nyssa's thirteenth NPNF letter concerning church order and the choice of a bishop.

nodes.name: Bishop of Melitene addressed by Gregory of Nyssa
nodes.bio: The bishop of Melitene is the recipient of Gregory of Nyssa's fourteenth NPNF letter.

nodes.name: Adelphius the Lawyer
nodes.bio: Adelphius the lawyer is the recipient of Gregory of Nyssa's fifteenth NPNF letter.

nodes.name: Amphilochius of Iconium
nodes.bio: Amphilochius of Iconium (c. 340-c. 400) was bishop of Iconium and a major Cappadocian churchman. Gregory of Nyssa addressed him in the sixteenth NPNF letter.

nodes.name: Eustathia, Ambrosia, and Basilissa
nodes.bio: Eustathia, Ambrosia, and Basilissa are the devout women named as recipients of Gregory of Nyssa's seventeenth NPNF letter.

nodes.name: Flavian of Antioch
nodes.bio: Flavian of Antioch (d. 404) was bishop of Antioch in the late fourth century. Gregory of Nyssa's eighteenth NPNF letter is addressed to Flavian.

nodes.name: Ursulus of Trier
nodes.bio: Ursulus was a grammarian at Trier known from Ausonius' letter about the New Year's bounty he had not received from the emperor.

nodes.name: Titus Ampius Balbus
nodes.bio: Titus Ampius Balbus was a Roman politician and Pompeian supporter addressed by Cicero during the civil-war period.

nodes.name: Quintus Ancharius
nodes.bio: Quintus Ancharius was a Roman proconsular recipient in Cicero's recommendation correspondence.

nodes.name: Gaius Antonius Hybrida
nodes.bio: Gaius Antonius Hybrida was Cicero's consular colleague in 63 BC and later a provincial commander addressed in Cicero's correspondence.

nodes.name: Lucius Minucius Basilus
nodes.bio: Lucius Minucius Basilus was a Roman politician associated with the conspiracy against Caesar and addressed by Cicero shortly after the Ides of March.

nodes.name: Publius Caesius
nodes.bio: Publius Caesius appears as a recipient in Cicero's recommendation correspondence.

nodes.name: Caninius Sallustius
nodes.bio: Caninius Sallustius was a Roman office-holder connected with Cicero's Cilician command. Ad Familiares 2.17 addresses him as proquaestor.

nodes.name: Marcus Cluvius
nodes.bio: Marcus Cluvius was a Roman businessman and correspondent in Cicero's recommendation network.

nodes.name: Gaius Coelius Caldus
nodes.bio: Gaius Coelius Caldus was Cicero's quaestor in Cilicia in 50 BC. Ad Familiares 2.19 addresses him in that administrative setting.

nodes.name: Furius Crassipes
nodes.bio: Furius Crassipes was a Roman aristocrat connected with Cicero's family and correspondence.

nodes.name: Marcus Licinius Crassus
nodes.bio: Marcus Licinius Crassus (c. 115-53 BC) was a Roman aristocrat, commander, and member of the first triumvirate, addressed by Cicero in Ad Familiares.

nodes.name: Manius Curius
nodes.bio: Manius Curius was a Roman businessman and friend of Cicero, known from Cicero's correspondence as part of the wider Italian and Greek commercial network.

nodes.name: Gaius Curtius Peducaeanus
nodes.bio: Gaius Curtius Peducaeanus was a Roman praetor and recipient in Cicero's recommendation correspondence.

nodes.name: Deiotarus
nodes.bio: Deiotarus was king of Galatia and a Roman ally, addressed in Cicero's recommendation correspondence.

nodes.name: Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus
nodes.bio: Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus (d. 48 BC) was a Roman senator, consul, and Pompeian commander addressed in Cicero's correspondence.

nodes.name: Publius Nigidius Figulus
nodes.bio: Publius Nigidius Figulus (c. 98-45 BC) was a Roman senator, scholar, and republican figure addressed by Cicero in exile-related correspondence.

nodes.name: Titus Furfanius Postumus
nodes.bio: Titus Furfanius Postumus was a Roman proconsular recipient in Cicero's correspondence, addressed in connection with Aulus Caecina.

nodes.name: Servius Sulpicius Galba
nodes.bio: Servius Sulpicius Galba was a Roman commander and correspondent of Cicero during the Mutina campaign.

nodes.name: Lucius Valerius, jurist
nodes.bio: Lucius Valerius was a jurist addressed by Cicero in Ad Familiares 1.10. The salutation identifies him by praenomen, nomen, and professional role.

nodes.name: Lucius Mescinius Rufus
nodes.bio: Lucius Mescinius Rufus served with Cicero in Cilicia and appears in Cicero's correspondence after that governorship.

nodes.name: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Nepos
nodes.bio: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Nepos (c. 100-55 BC) was a Roman senator and political opponent turned correspondent of Cicero.

nodes.name: Gaius Munatius
nodes.bio: Gaius Munatius appears as a named recipient in Cicero's recommendation correspondence.

nodes.name: Gaius Oppius
nodes.bio: Gaius Oppius was a Roman equestrian, friend of Caesar, and correspondent in Cicero's late republican network.

nodes.name: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus
nodes.bio: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus (106-48 BC), known as Pompey, was one of the dominant Roman commanders and politicians of the late Republic and a major figure in Cicero's political world.

nodes.name: Marcus Rutilius
nodes.bio: Marcus Rutilius appears in Cicero's recommendation correspondence as a named recipient.

nodes.name: Publius Sestius
nodes.role: Tribune of the plebs, Cicero supporter
nodes.bio: Publius Sestius was a Roman politician and supporter of Cicero, known from Cicero's defense speech for him and from the correspondence.

nodes.name: Gaius Sextilius Rufus
nodes.bio: Gaius Sextilius Rufus was a quaestorian recipient in Cicero's recommendation correspondence.

nodes.name: Publius Sittius
nodes.bio: Publius Sittius was a Roman financier and military adventurer connected with Cicero's network and recommendation correspondence.

nodes.name: Publius Sulpicius Rufus
nodes.bio: Publius Sulpicius Rufus appears as an imperator addressed by Cicero in Ad Familiares book 13.
