nodes.name: Longinus Priscus
nodes.bio: Longinus Priscus was a Roman military or administrative patron addressed by Claudius Tiberianus in P.Mich. VIII 472. Tiberianus calls him his lord and patron, asks where he is stationed, and hopes to reach him after missing the boats from Alexandria. The letter also links Longinus with Sempronius Clemens, a frumentarius who was to carry correspondence.

nodes.name: Papirius Apollinarius
nodes.role: Roman Egyptian correspondent in the Tiberianus archive
nodes.bio: Papirius Apollinarius wrote to Claudius Tiberianus in P.Mich. VIII 475. His short Greek letter asks Tiberianus to investigate what Gaius sold, who inherited from the deceased Sextus, and when Sextus's will would be opened. The address identifies Tiberianus as a veteran.

nodes.name: Tasoucharion
nodes.role: Roman Egyptian woman and papyrus-letter recipient
nodes.bio: Tasoucharion was the sister addressed by Claudius Terentianus in P.Mich. VIII 481. The letter places her inside the household network of the Claudius Tiberianus archive at Karanis and asks her to receive baskets, respond about health and needs, arrange supplies, and pass greetings through a circle of family and local contacts.

nodes.name: Taeis
nodes.role: Roman Egyptian woman and papyrus letter writer
nodes.bio: Taeis was the sender of P.Mich. VIII 510, a Greek papyrus letter to her son and lord. She writes from the family orbit of Alexandria and Karanis about money, documents, irrigation of date-palms, public dues, grief or death in Alexandria, and her dependence on her absent son's management of household affairs.

nodes.name: Unnamed son of Taeis
nodes.bio: The unnamed son of Taeis is the recipient of P.Mich. VIII 510. Taeis addresses him as her son and lord, asks for news of his safety, and credits him with managing her affairs while absent, including public payments, documents, and property matters connected with Karanis.

nodes.name: Valerius Paulinus alias Ammonas
nodes.role: Roman soldier and papyrus letter writer
nodes.bio: Valerius Paulinus, also called Ammonas, was a Roman soldier known from SB VI 9636. Writing in AD 136 to his brother Valerius Apollinarius, he expects discharge after one more year of service and gives instructions about a tenant, house use, field leasing, and purchases to be made through his brother.

nodes.name: Valerius Apollinarius
nodes.role: Roman Egyptian recipient of SB VI 9636
nodes.bio: Valerius Apollinarius was the brother and recipient of SB VI 9636, sent by Valerius Paulinus alias Ammonas in AD 136. The letter asks him to receive Terentianus, oversee arrangements for house and field leasing, and purchase household goods from a linen-seller near the temple.

nodes.name: Caesarius and Eubulus
nodes.bio: Caesarius and Eubulus are the joint recipients of Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 1. Procopius teases them for their silence, comparing their failure to answer letters with the disciplined silence of Pythagoras.

nodes.name: Pythius, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Pythius is the recipient of Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 3. Procopius praises him as a man inhabited by the Muses and apologizes that a desired book has not yet arrived from Alexandria.

nodes.name: Germanus, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Germanus is the recipient of Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 4. The letter praises the pleasure of meeting him and complains, warmly, that his absence has only increased Procopius's longing for renewed company.

nodes.name: Alypius, Stephen, and Hierius
nodes.bio: Alypius, Stephen, and Hierius are the joint recipients of Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 13. The heading identifies Alypius and Stephen as grammarians and Hierius as Roman; the letter places the group near Daphne, where Procopius imagines them amid Apollo's spring, trees, shade, and mythic associations.

nodes.name: Strategius and Ilasius
nodes.bio: Strategius and Ilasius are the joint recipients of Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 20. Procopius thanks them for sending fish and turns the gift into a playful comparison between fertile vineyards, generous character, and a sea that serves their liberality.

nodes.name: Eusebius, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Eusebius is addressed by Procopius of Gaza in Epistles 20 and 79, and appears in a joint letter with Elias. The letters show him within a circle of education, shared affection, and concern for a young man's formation.

nodes.name: Victor, brother of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Victor, addressed as brother in Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 28, sent a desired book to Procopius. The reply turns thanks for the book into a reflection on memory, gratitude, and the betrayal of Pausanias.

nodes.name: Unknown recipient of Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 30
nodes.role: Unidentified recipient of a consolation letter
nodes.bio: The recipient of Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 30 is not preserved in the source heading. The letter consoles someone after the death of a young woman before marriage, urging philosophical acceptance without minimizing the grief.

nodes.name: Constantius, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Constantius is the recipient of Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 48. Procopius describes receiving his letter while still near the Nile and being moved by the illusion that Constantius himself had arrived.

nodes.name: Athenodorus, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Book lender and purchaser of property or rights
nodes.bio: Athenodorus is the recipient of Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 63. After receiving a book from him, Procopius reports that he has arranged for Athenodorus to purchase the part of a possession he needs.

nodes.name: Castor, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Advocate or patron asked to help a kinsman
nodes.bio: Castor is the recipient of Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 73. Procopius asks him to use just speech and legal skill for a bearer connected to Procopius by kinship and marriage.

nodes.name: Irenaeus, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Kinsman or patron of young men commended to Procopius
nodes.bio: Irenaeus is the recipient of Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 78. Procopius credits him with first creating goodwill toward the young men around Zonaios, then says their own character confirmed that goodwill.

nodes.name: Eusebius and Elias, correspondents of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Joint correspondents and guardians of a shared student
nodes.bio: Eusebius and Elias are jointly addressed in Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 79. Procopius sends a shared young student to them with a letter and prays that the young man's education will fulfill their hopes.

nodes.name: Phaedrus, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Correspondent whose letter reveals paternal affection
nodes.bio: Phaedrus is the recipient of Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 80. Procopius says Phaedrus's letter shows the image of his soul and reads like the writing of an affectionate father to a child.

nodes.name: Agapetus, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Rhetorical correspondent at or near Elusa
nodes.bio: Agapetus is addressed by Procopius of Gaza in Epistle 87. Procopius teases him for turning an expected accusation back on his friends after leaving Alexandria and being reported present near Elusa.

nodes.name: Apollonius, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Patron or helper asked to support Martyrius
nodes.bio: Apollonius is addressed by Procopius of Gaza in Epistle 93. Procopius asks him to help the reverent Martyrius and to make good Martyrius's confidence that a letter from Procopius would secure assistance.

nodes.name: Macarius, correspondent and bearer of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Bearer, student of law, and correspondent
nodes.bio: Macarius appears in Procopius of Gaza, Epistles 96 and 97. He carries Silanus's letter and then receives a reply praising a sweet gift, his friendship across distance, and his study of the laws.

nodes.name: Antiochus, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Medical or philosophical correspondent in Alexandria
nodes.bio: Antiochus is addressed by Procopius of Gaza in Epistle 104. Procopius expected him to leave medical business behind and come for philosophy, but instead finds him lingering in Alexandria among the city's charms.

nodes.name: Sosianus and Julius, correspondents of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Joint correspondents of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Sosianus and Julius are jointly addressed in Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 107. Procopius turns their letter into a comic reversal of an astrologer's promise of sudden good fortune.

nodes.name: Nonnus, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Correspondent wavering between marriage and priesthood
nodes.bio: Nonnus is addressed by Procopius of Gaza in Epistle 112. Procopius jokes that his beautiful hair may keep him circling between a bride and priestly ordination.

nodes.name: Hieronymus and Theodorus, correspondents of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Hieronymus and Theodorus are jointly addressed in Procopius of Gaza, Epistle 113. Procopius praises their family's legal and rhetorical pedigree while explaining why loyalty to his own city keeps him from taking another's place.

nodes.name: Hermeias, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Civic patron or official associated with Berytus
nodes.bio: Hermeias is addressed by Procopius of Gaza in Epistle 114. Procopius praises him as a man whose letter reveals concern for virtue, letters, and the civic adornment of Berytus.

nodes.name: Anatolius, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Pious correspondent asked to support a young man
nodes.bio: Anatolius is addressed by Procopius of Gaza in Epistle 116. The letter commends a young man to him on the strength of Anatolius's piety, the young man's father, professional obligation, and divine help.

nodes.name: Marcellus, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Correspondent asked to release a virtuous visitor
nodes.bio: Marcellus is addressed by Procopius of Gaza in Epistle 130. Procopius asks him not to detain a virtuous man recently arrived from Egypt, because the man is anxious to keep promises and report Marcellus's kindness.

nodes.name: Peter, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Peter is addressed by Procopius of Gaza in Epistle 135. Procopius responds to Peter's recommendation of Epiphanius, praises the young man's zeal for learning, and treats his conduct as an answer to slander.

nodes.name: Nilus, beneficiary of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Correspondent and beneficiary of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Nilus appears as a beneficiary in a property dispute and as a correspondent whose lavish praise gives Procopius occasion to joke about rhetoric, money, and the sale of words.

nodes.name: Eudaemon, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Eudaemon is addressed by Procopius of Gaza as a just legal patron. Procopius recommends Hierius to him and praises the restoration of justice under his voice.

nodes.name: Sozomen, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Student and correspondent praised for zeal
nodes.bio: Sozomen is praised through a report from Caesarius. Procopius rejoices that a good witness describes his zeal for words and self-control.

nodes.name: Zosimus and Macarius, correspondents of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Zosimus and Macarius are jointly addressed by Procopius of Gaza after reports from the circle of Babylas. He expects their legal training to preserve the discipline and self-control they showed with him.

nodes.name: Evagrius, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Evagrius writes such extravagant praise that Procopius answers with comic embarrassment, comparing love's distortion of judgment to making Thersites beautiful.

nodes.name: Cledonius, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Correspondent and father of a prospective student
nodes.bio: Cledonius praises Procopius with such force that Procopius jokes he may mistakenly write Cledonius's name on letters to others. The letter also concerns a young man whom Procopius promises to teach with goodwill.

nodes.name: Megethius, correspondent of Procopius of Gaza
nodes.role: Rhetorical admirer and sender to Procopius of Gaza
nodes.bio: Megethius writes to Procopius of Gaza after hearing and praising his funeral oration. His letter asks Procopius to send the speech so those who missed it may enjoy it.

nodes.name: Magnus, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Magnus was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 26. Chrysostom writes first to Magnus and asks for news of his health and church care.

nodes.name: Domnus, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Domnus was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 27. Chrysostom thanks Domnus for sending a presbyter and says loving letters ease bodily separation.

nodes.name: Basil, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Basil was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 28. Chrysostom praises Basil's pastoral zeal against pagan error and asks for reports of his work.

nodes.name: Hortius, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Hortius was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 30. Chrysostom asks Hortius for health updates and describes the desolation and danger of Cucusus.

nodes.name: Maron, presbyter and monk, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Maron was a presbyter and monk addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 36. Chrysostom tells Maron that love sees across distance and asks for prayers and news.

nodes.name: Candidianus, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Candidianus was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 42. Chrysostom tells Candidianus that distance, raids, illness, and solitude have not weakened love.

nodes.name: Bassiana, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Bassiana was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 43. Chrysostom trusts Bassiana's love despite silence and asks for news of her household.

nodes.name: Symmachus, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Symmachus was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 45. Chrysostom consoles Symmachus that virtue's hard road leads to lasting rewards.

nodes.name: Rufinus, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Rufinus was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 46. Chrysostom says he loves Rufinus continually even when roads and season prevent frequent writing.

nodes.name: Namaia, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Namaia was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 47. Chrysostom playfully accepts Namaia's letter but complains that it came late.

nodes.name: Gerontius, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Gerontius was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 54. Chrysostom urges Gerontius to go quickly to Phoenicia before winter closes the road.

nodes.name: Symeon and Maris, presbyters and monks near Apamea
nodes.bio: Symeon and Maris was a presbyters and monks addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 55. Chrysostom asks presbyters and monks near Apamea for prayers, letters, and helpers for John in Phoenicia.

nodes.name: Romulus and Byzus, monks and correspondents of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Romulus and Byzus was a monks addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 56. Chrysostom says love can bind unseen friends across winter roads and asks the monks for news.

nodes.name: Theodosius, former dux and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Theodosius was a former dux addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 58. Chrysostom compares Theodosius's letter to honey and asks for continued news of his household.

nodes.name: Theodotus, former consularis and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Theodotus was a former consularis addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 61. Chrysostom sends away Theodotus's son because Armenia is too dangerous and asks care for the boy.

nodes.name: Aphthonius, Theodotus, and Chaereas, presbyters and monks
nodes.bio: Aphthonius, Theodotus, and Chaereas was a presbyters and monks addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 70. Chrysostom asks Aphthonius, Theodotus, and Chaereas for prayers and letters amid siege and illness.

nodes.name: Malchus, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Malchus was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 71. Chrysostom consoles Malchus and his wife on the death of their daughter.

nodes.name: Harmatius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Harmatius was a correspondent and patron addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 75. Chrysostom asks Harmatius for letters rather than material help through servants.

nodes.name: Gemellus, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Gemellus was a officeholder and correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 79. Chrysostom playfully asks Gemellus to solve the riddle of his silence after gaining office.

nodes.name: Firminus, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Firminus was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 80. Chrysostom tells Firminus that illness prevented a meeting but not friendship, and reports safe arrival.

nodes.name: Cytherius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Cytherius was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 82. Chrysostom says a brief meeting created lasting friendship and asks Cytherius for health news.

nodes.name: Leontius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Leontius was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 83. Chrysostom says exile removed him from Leontius's city but not from his love.

nodes.name: Faustinus, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Faustinus was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 84. Chrysostom reports his safe arrival at Cucusus and asks Faustinus for letters.

nodes.name: Lucius, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Lucius was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 85. Chrysostom praises Lucius for rejecting the church disorders and urges continued courage.

nodes.name: Maras, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Maras was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 86. Chrysostom praises Maras's steady judgment during the church crisis and asks him to encourage others.

nodes.name: Eulogius, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Eulogius was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 87. Chrysostom remembers Eulogius's virtue from Cucusus and praises his stand for the churches.

nodes.name: John, bishop of Jerusalem
nodes.bio: John of Jerusalem was a bishop of Jerusalem addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 88. Chrysostom urges John of Jerusalem to continue separating from those who disturbed the churches.

nodes.name: Severus, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Severus was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 101. Chrysostom asks Severus to break a long silence and write directly about his health.

nodes.name: Urbicius, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Urbicius was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 108. Chrysostom tells Urbicius that genuine love is not dimmed by time or the dangers around Cucusus.

nodes.name: Rufinus, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Rufinus was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 109. Chrysostom recalls Rufinus from Antioch and asks him to remember the exile in Cucusus.

nodes.name: Bassus, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Bassus was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 110. Chrysostom gently rebukes Bassus for not writing despite their friendship and proximity.

nodes.name: Anatolius, bishop of Adana
nodes.bio: Anatolius of Adana was a bishop of Adana addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 111. Chrysostom writes to Anatolius of Adana after hearing of his love from others.

nodes.name: Theodore, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Theodore was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 112. Chrysostom thanks Theodore for efforts on his behalf and asks him to keep love in bloom.

nodes.name: Palladius, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Palladius was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 113. Chrysostom asks Palladius for prayers over the storm afflicting the churches.

nodes.name: Bishops and presbyters in prison
nodes.bio: Bishops and presbyters in prison was a imprisoned clergy addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 118. Chrysostom congratulates imprisoned bishops and presbyters on suffering chains for God.

nodes.name: Marcianus, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Marcianus was a patron and correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 122. Chrysostom praises Marcianus for supporting widows, orphans, and the poor during the crisis.

nodes.name: Presbyters and monks in Phoenicia catechizing pagans
nodes.bio: Presbyters and monks in Phoenicia was a presbyters and monks addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 123. Chrysostom urges the clergy and monks teaching in Phoenicia not to abandon their work during the storm.

nodes.name: Cyriacus, bishop in exile and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Cyriacus was a bishop in exile addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 125. Chrysostom consoles the exiled bishop Cyriacus with examples of endurance and urges him to cast off despondency.

nodes.name: Rufinus, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Rufinus was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 126. Chrysostom urges Rufinus to go quickly to Phoenicia after renewed attacks on monks there.

nodes.name: Marinianus, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Marinianus was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 128. Chrysostom celebrates spring because it reopens letter-writing after winter closed the roads.

nodes.name: Theodore, consular of Syria and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Theodore was a consular of Syria addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 139. Chrysostom asks Theodore not to measure love by the number of letters.

nodes.name: Theodotus, former consular and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Theodotus was a churchman and correspondent of John Chrysostom, appearing as lector or deacon in the PG 52 Epistulae. Chrysostom writes to him about health, travel, friendship, and endurance during the exile crisis.

nodes.name: Nicholas, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Nicholas was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 145. Chrysostom asks Nicholas for health news as consolation in daily fear and illness.

nodes.name: Theodotus, Nicholas, and Chaerea, presbyters and monks
nodes.bio: Theodotus, Nicholas, and Chaerea was a presbyters and monks addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 146. Chrysostom says love makes the absent clergy present and asks them for prayers and letters.

nodes.name: Anthemius, imperial official and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Anthemius was a imperial official addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 147. Chrysostom says Anthemius adorns his offices and will become a harbor for the wronged.

nodes.name: Cyriacus, Demetrius, Palladius, and Eulysius, bishops
nodes.bio: Cyriacus, Demetrius, Palladius, and Eulysius was a bishops addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 148. Chrysostom praises four bishops for laboring for church peace and commends John and Paul to them.

nodes.name: Aurelius, bishop of Carthage
nodes.bio: Aurelius of Carthage was a bishop of Carthage addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 149. Chrysostom praises Aurelius of Carthage for laboring to bring troubled churches into peace.

nodes.name: Maximus, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Maximus was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 150. Chrysostom thanks Maximus for long labor and watchfulness in correcting the church crisis.

nodes.name: Asellus, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Asellus was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 151. Chrysostom urges Asellus to keep helping the churches of the East through counsel, prayer, and action.

nodes.name: Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia
nodes.bio: Chromatius of Aquileia was a bishop of Aquileia addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 155. Chrysostom praises Chromatius of Aquileia for love, boldness, and care for the churches.

nodes.name: A bishop from the West and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: A bishop from the West was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 160. Chrysostom thanks a western bishop for laboring at home and across the sea for the churches.

nodes.name: Roman presbyters who came with western bishops
nodes.bio: Roman presbyters was a presbyters from Rome addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 161. Chrysostom thanks Roman presbyters for crossing the sea in support of the churches.

nodes.name: Anysius, bishop of Thessalonica
nodes.bio: Anysius of Thessalonica was a bishop of Thessalonica addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 162. Chrysostom apologizes to Anysius for late writing and thanks him for his church zeal.

nodes.name: Anysius and orthodox bishops in Macedonia
nodes.bio: Anysius and Macedonian bishops was a bishops in Macedonia addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 163. Chrysostom urges Anysius and Macedonian bishops to finish their long stand with courage.

nodes.name: Alexander, bishop of Corinth
nodes.bio: Alexander of Corinth was a bishop of Corinth addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 164. Chrysostom writes to Alexander of Corinth as a beloved ally in the church crisis.

nodes.name: Proba, freedwoman in Rome and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Proba was a freedwoman in Rome addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 168. Chrysostom tells Proba that distance cannot hide her warm love and zeal.

nodes.name: Juliana and her companions, correspondents of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Juliana and her companions was a women correspondents addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 169. Chrysostom encourages Juliana and her companions to endure for the greater reward.

nodes.name: Italica, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Italica was a woman correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 170. Chrysostom tells Italica that women and men share the same contests and crowns in virtue.

nodes.name: Montius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Montius was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 171. Chrysostom says he is far from Montius in body but near through affection and memory.

nodes.name: Helladius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Helladius was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 172. Chrysostom says a brief meeting with Helladius proved his genuine love.

nodes.name: Euethius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Euethius was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 173. Chrysostom tells Euethius that bodily separation has not broken their bond of love.

nodes.name: Bishops, presbyters, and deacons confined in Chalcedon
nodes.bio: Clergy confined in Chalcedon was a bishops, presbyters, and deacons addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 174. Chrysostom blesses clergy confined in Chalcedon for bearing chains with apostolic courage.

nodes.name: Artemidorus, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Artemidorus was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 177. Chrysostom commends Antiochus to Artemidorus and asks Artemidorus for health news.

nodes.name: Bishops addressed by John Chrysostom in Epistula 181
nodes.bio: Bishops addressed collectively was a bishops addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 181. Chrysostom praises bishops who keep trying to correct the eastern church crisis despite delays.

nodes.name: Venerius, bishop of Milan
nodes.bio: Venerius of Milan was a bishop of Milan addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 182. Chrysostom urges Venerius of Milan to keep using bold zeal for the troubled churches.

nodes.name: Gaudentius, bishop of Brixia
nodes.bio: Gaudentius of Brixia was a bishop of Brixia addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 184. Chrysostom thanks Gaudentius of Brixia for vigilance and labor on behalf of truth.

nodes.name: Alypius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Alypius was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 186. Chrysostom tells Alypius that writing first is a sign of love, not forwardness.

nodes.name: Procopius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Procopius was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 187. Chrysostom remembers Procopius's genuine love and asks him to write about his health.

nodes.name: Antiochus, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Antiochus was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 189. Chrysostom says he carries Antiochus's warm love with him even at the world's edge.

nodes.name: Onesicratia, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Onesicratia was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 192. Chrysostom consoles Onesicratia after the death of her daughter.

nodes.name: Gemellus, imperial official and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Gemellus was an imperial official addressed by John Chrysostom in the PG 52 Epistulae. Chrysostom praises his public authority, concern for justice, and continuing friendship during the exile crisis.

nodes.name: Claudianus, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Claudianus was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 195. Chrysostom playfully rebukes Claudianus for a long silence and demands a letter.

nodes.name: Aetius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Aetius was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 196. Chrysostom tells Aetius that letters from friends console exile, illness, and danger.

nodes.name: Studius, urban prefect and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Studius was a urban prefect addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 197. Chrysostom consoles Studius on the death of his brother and urges measured grief.

nodes.name: Daniel, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Daniel was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 199. Chrysostom praises Daniel for bearing affliction with joy and asks for frequent news.

nodes.name: Callistratus, bishop of Isauria
nodes.bio: Callistratus of Isauria was a bishop of Isauria addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 200. Chrysostom thanks Callistratus for writing first and hopes for a visit when travel allows.

nodes.name: Herculius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Herculius was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 201. Chrysostom dismisses excuses for Herculius's silence while still asking for health news.

nodes.name: Salustius, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Salustius was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 203. Chrysostom warns Salustius against slack preaching during persecution.

nodes.name: Anatolius, praetorian prefect and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Anatolius was a praetorian prefect addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 205. Chrysostom explains that illness delayed his writing to Anatolius and asks for health news.

nodes.name: Theodulus, deacon and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Theodulus was a deacon addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 206. Chrysostom urges Theodulus to keep preventing disturbance in Gothia and to pray for peace.

nodes.name: Gothic monks in the region of Promotus
nodes.bio: Gothic monks in Promotus was a monks addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 207. Chrysostom encourages Gothic monks enduring plots and insults while preventing church disturbance.

nodes.name: Acacius, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Acacius was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 208. Chrysostom urges Acacius to write quickly with news of his health.

nodes.name: Salvian, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Salvian was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 209. Chrysostom asks Salvian for news of his health, his wife's health, and his whole household.

nodes.name: Theodore, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Theodore was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 210. Chrysostom asks Theodore to rouse Salustius from slackness during the church crisis.

nodes.name: Timothy, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Timothy was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 211. Chrysostom thanks Timothy for zeal and endurance in danger.

nodes.name: Philip, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Philip was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 213. Chrysostom praises Philip after expulsion from the school and asks for news of his health.

nodes.name: Sebastianus, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Sebastianus was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 214. Chrysostom tells Sebastianus that love overcomes bodily separation and asks for health news.

nodes.name: Pelagius, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Pelagius was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 215. Chrysostom praises Pelagius's kindness and asks for continuing news of his health.

nodes.name: Musonius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Musonius was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 216. Chrysostom writes despite Musonius's silence and describes winter, robbers, and scarce carriers.

nodes.name: Euthymius, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Euthymius was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 218. Chrysostom encourages Euthymius after expulsion from the school and asks for letters.

nodes.name: Severina and Romula, correspondents of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Severina and Romula was a correspondents addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 219. Chrysostom gently complains of Severina and Romula's silence while trusting their love.

nodes.name: Theodore the physician, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Theodore the physician was a physician addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 228. Chrysostom tells Theodore the physician that love makes him present despite his busyness.

nodes.name: Severa, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Severa was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 229. Chrysostom writes to Severa after hearing from Libanius about her zeal for the faith.

nodes.name: Bishop of Antioch addressed by John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: This unnamed bishop of Antioch is addressed in PG 52 Epistulae 233, where the writer protests slander, exclusion from the church, and the failure of friends to investigate the truth.

nodes.name: Porphyrius, bishop of Rhosus
nodes.bio: Porphyrius of Rhosus was a bishop of Rhosus addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 235. Chrysostom thanks Porphyrius for steadfast love from near Cucusus.

nodes.name: Carterius, governor and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Carterius was a governor addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 236. Chrysostom thanks Carterius for restraining disturbances and describes Cucusus as quiet harbor.

nodes.name: Mother of Constantius, presbyter
nodes.bio: The mother of Constantius is praised in PG 52 Epistulae 237 for urging her son to choose conscience and exile over improper compromise.

nodes.name: Sister of Constantius, presbyter
nodes.bio: The sister of Constantius is addressed in PG 52 Epistulae 238 as a woman whose household cares, poverty, and family distress are turned into occasions for endurance.

nodes.name: Valerius and Diophantus, presbyters of Antioch
nodes.bio: Valerius and Diophantus was a presbyters of Antioch addressed by Constantius in PG 52 Epistulae 239. Constantius asks Valerius and Diophantus for letters and encourages them to endure for truth.

nodes.name: Castus, presbyter and correspondent of Constantius
nodes.bio: Castus was a presbyter in the Antiochene network around John Chrysostom and Constantius. He appears among Antiochene presbyters in PG 52 Epistulae 222 and is addressed by Constantius in ep.240.

nodes.name: Cyriacus, presbyter and correspondent of Constantius
nodes.bio: Cyriacus was a presbyter in the Antiochene network around John Chrysostom and Constantius. He appears among Antiochene presbyters in PG 52 Epistulae 222 and is addressed by Constantius in ep.241.

nodes.name: John, correspondent of Aeneas of Gaza
nodes.bio: John is the recipient of Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 1, a playful request for the return of a prized book.

nodes.name: Cassus, correspondent of Aeneas of Gaza
nodes.bio: Cassus is addressed in Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 2, where Aeneas urges him to leave rustic isolation and return to the conversations of the city.

nodes.name: Alphius the Presbyter
nodes.bio: Alphius the Presbyter receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 3, a compact legal admonition over a disputed estate.

nodes.name: Zonainus the Sophist
nodes.bio: Zonainus is praised indirectly through Epiphanius in Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 4, where character matters more than rhetorical skill.

nodes.name: Ulpius, correspondent of Aeneas of Gaza
nodes.bio: Ulpius receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 5, a consolation after robbery that contrasts fragile wealth with durable learning.

nodes.name: Pampus the Grammarian
nodes.bio: Pampus the Grammarian receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 6, a short consolation that treats a friend's loss as shared property.

nodes.name: Zosimus, leading citizen and correspondent of Aeneas of Gaza
nodes.bio: Zosimus, described as a leading citizen, receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 8 after a voyage undertaken for friends rather than trade or piracy.

nodes.name: Sopater the Sophist
nodes.bio: Sopater receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 9, which asks help for Constantine, a wandering poet seeking support.

nodes.name: Zosimus the Sophist
nodes.bio: Zosimus the Sophist receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 10, recommending the elderly poet Paul as a worthy object of honor.

nodes.name: Marinianus, former consul
nodes.bio: Marinianus, a former consul, receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 11, recommending the industrious student Ponto.

nodes.name: Encratius, correspondent of Aeneas of Gaza
nodes.bio: Encratius receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 13, an appeal to help a fallen teacher with the same solidarity soldiers show one another.

nodes.name: John the Presbyter, correspondent of Aeneas of Gaza
nodes.bio: John the Presbyter receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 14, which turns a gift of vegetables into praise of gentle educational discipline.

nodes.name: Stephen the Presbyter
nodes.bio: Stephen the Presbyter receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 15, where memories of playful rhetoric by the Nile lead into praise of Stephen's serious preaching.

nodes.name: Sarapion, correspondent of Aeneas of Gaza
nodes.bio: Sarapion receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 16, a reflection on conflict among priests, courage under trial, and the love of rhetoric.

nodes.name: Dionysius the Sophist
nodes.bio: Dionysius the Sophist receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 17, recommending a student to a city imagined as a new school of the Muses.

nodes.name: Theodorus the Sophist
nodes.bio: Theodorus the Sophist receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 18, a praise of Syrian Atticism and rhetorical fame.

nodes.name: Dorotheus the Presbyter
nodes.bio: Dorotheus the Presbyter receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 21, asking practical help for a sacred minister seeking quiet on a holy mountain.

nodes.name: Marcianus, correspondent of Aeneas of Gaza
nodes.bio: Marcianus receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 24, a request for justice and relief after the bearer is robbed while trying to buy palm produce.

nodes.name: Julian the Architect
nodes.bio: Julian the Architect receives Aeneas of Gaza, Letter 25, a technical but playful note about improving a water-lifting machine.

nodes.name: Theodosius, bishop of Scythopolis
nodes.bio: Theodosius of Scythopolis was a bishop of Scythopolis addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 89. Chrysostom tells Theodosius that love crosses distance and urges him to reject those disturbing the churches.

nodes.name: Moses, bishop and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Moses was a bishop addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 90. Chrysostom urges Bishop Moses to keep separating from those who harmed the churches and to encourage others.

nodes.name: Moses, presbyter and correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Moses was a presbyter addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 92. Chrysostom asks Moses the presbyter to pray for the churches and to write often about his health.

nodes.name: Aphthonius, Theodotus, Chaereas, and their community
nodes.bio: Aphthonius, Theodotus, Chaereas, and their community was a presbyters, monastics, and community addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 93. Chrysostom asks a monastic and clerical community to support him through prayer across distance.

nodes.name: Paeanius, correspondent of John Chrysostom
nodes.bio: Paeanius was a correspondent addressed by John Chrysostom in PG 52 Epistulae 95. Chrysostom tells Paeanius to mourn the persecutors rather than the sufferers and asks for health news.

nodes.name: Honoratus, Donatist bishop
nodes.bio: Honoratus was a Donatist bishop who, according to Augustine, agreed to discuss Christian peace by letter rather than through public disorder.

nodes.name: Severinus, kinsman of Augustine
nodes.role: Donatist Christian and kinsman of Augustine
nodes.bio: Severinus was a relative of Augustine who remained in Donatist communion. Augustine appealed to their blood relationship while urging him toward unity in Christ.

nodes.name: Naucelio, Donatist interlocutor
nodes.bio: Naucelio was a Donatist interlocutor addressed jointly by Alypius and Augustine in a letter about Felicianus of Musti and the logic of rebaptism.

nodes.name: Macrobius, Donatist bishop of Hippo
nodes.bio: Macrobius was a Donatist bishop in the Hippo region. Augustine wrote to him in 409 urging him not to rebaptize a catholic subdeacon.

nodes.name: Maximus and Theodorus, correspondents of Augustine
nodes.bio: Maximus and Theodorus reported back to Augustine after delivering his letter to the Donatist bishop Macrobius.

nodes.name: Cresconius, correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Cresconius was a correspondent whom Augustine asked to support a petition for Faventius, a man who had sought the church's protection.

nodes.name: Florentinus, official of the count
nodes.role: official attached to a Roman count
nodes.bio: Florentinus was an official involved in the custody of Faventius. Augustine wrote to him asking that imperial law be applied with humanity.

nodes.name: Hilarius of Syracuse
nodes.bio: Hilarius wrote from the Syracuse context to ask Augustine about doctrinal claims associated with sinlessness, baptism, wealth, oaths, and the church.

nodes.name: Timasius and Jacobus
nodes.bio: Timasius and Jacobus thanked Augustine for his treatise On Nature and Grace, which answered Pelagian claims about nature and divine grace.

nodes.name: Claudius, bishop and correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Claudius was a bishop who sent Augustine Julian's books against him, prompting Augustine to share his own reply for Claudius's judgment.

nodes.name: Chrisimus, correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Chrisimus was a Christian correspondent whom Augustine consoled after a severe worldly loss, urging him to locate hope in God rather than possessions.

nodes.name: Restitutus, deacon and correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Restitutus was a deacon who shared Augustine's concern over scandals within the church and received counsel about patience and unity.

nodes.name: Pancarius, correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Pancarius was involved in a local church dispute around the presbyter Secundinus. Augustine urged him to keep accusations catholic, lawful, and nonviolent.

nodes.name: Felix, correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Felix was a correspondent involved in the care of an orphan girl entrusted to the church, a case Augustine handled cautiously.

nodes.name: Rusticus, correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Rusticus sought a marriage arrangement for his son. Augustine refused to promise a Christian girl while the son remained pagan.

nodes.name: Christinus, correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Christinus was a warm correspondent whose desire for Augustine's letters drew a brief spiritual maxim about difficult but fruitful work.

nodes.name: Orontius, correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Orontius wrote ahead of a visit to Augustine, turning travel and correspondence into a moment of mutual Christian courtesy.

nodes.name: Donatus, former proconsul and correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Donatus was a former proconsul and public official whom Augustine praised for upright administration while urging him toward Christ and catholic unity.

nodes.name: Hilarius, bishop and correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Hilarius was a fellow bishop whom Augustine warned about Pelagian teaching and the African council response against it.

nodes.name: Deuterius, bishop and correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Deuterius was a bishop whom Augustine warned about Victorinus, a subdeacon who had secretly taught Manichaean doctrine while appearing as catholic clergy.

nodes.name: Sebastianus, correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Sebastianus was a Christian correspondent whose grief over the wickedness of others led Augustine and Alypius to write about holy sorrow and perseverance.

nodes.name: Saturninus, Eufratus, and clerics returned to catholic unity
nodes.bio: Saturninus, Eufratus, and the clerics with them were ministers who returned from schism to catholic communion; Augustine wrote to confirm them in unity and faithful service.

nodes.name: Maxima, correspondent of Augustine
nodes.role: Christian woman and correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Maxima was a Christian woman who wrote to Augustine about dangerous errors troubling her province and asked for counsel on Christ's incarnation.

nodes.name: Florentina, student and correspondent of Augustine
nodes.role: Christian woman and student of sacred teaching
nodes.bio: Florentina was a young Christian woman whose parents told Augustine of her eagerness for true wisdom; Augustine invited her to send questions while reminding her that Christ teaches inwardly.

nodes.name: Council of Milevis bishops
nodes.bio: The Council of Milevis was a North African episcopal gathering whose bishops wrote to Rome in 416 against Pelagian teaching on grace, prayer, and infant baptism.

nodes.name: Martianus
nodes.role: old friend and catechumen addressed by Augustine
nodes.bio: Martianus was an old friend of Augustine whose entry among the catechumens led Augustine to write about true friendship, baptism, and shared life in Christ.

nodes.name: Apringius
nodes.bio: Apringius was proconsul of Africa when Augustine appealed to him for clemency toward violent Circumcellions and Donatist clerics who had confessed attacks on catholic clergy.

nodes.name: Cornelius
nodes.bio: Cornelius was a lay correspondent who asked Augustine for a consolatory praise of his dead wife Cypriana; Augustine instead urged him to imitate her chastity.

nodes.name: Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius
nodes.role: African bishops in the Pelagian controversy
nodes.bio: Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius were five African bishops who appealed to Innocent I of Rome during the Pelagian controversy.

nodes.name: Silvanus, Valentinus, and the Milevitan council bishops
nodes.role: North African bishops of the Milevitan council
nodes.bio: Silvanus, Valentinus, and the bishops gathered at Milevis wrote to Innocent I during the Pelagian controversy, seeking Roman confirmation of their judgment on grace, free choice, and infant baptism.

nodes.name: Seleuciana
nodes.role: Christian woman and correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Seleuciana was a Christian woman who asked Augustine to answer claims associated with a Novatian interlocutor about Peter, baptism, and repentance.

nodes.name: Maximus, physician and correspondent of Augustine
nodes.role: physician and recent convert from Arian teaching
nodes.bio: Maximus was a physician and correspondent whom Alypius and Augustine congratulate for entering catholic communion after leaving Arian teaching. They urge him to teach the same Trinitarian faith to his household and associates.

nodes.name: Ceretius, bishop and correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Ceretius was a bishop who sent Augustine writings that seemed to be connected with Priscillianist teaching. Augustine's reply warns him about apocryphal texts, secretive exegesis, and pastoral care for people wounded by heresy.

nodes.name: Ecdicia
nodes.role: Christian matron and correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Ecdicia was a married Christian woman who consulted Augustine about ascetic practice inside her household. Augustine's reply rebukes her for making unilateral decisions about continence, almsgiving, and dress that helped destabilize her husband and their shared vow.

nodes.name: Armentarius and Paulina
nodes.role: Christian married couple and correspondents of Augustine
nodes.bio: Armentarius and Paulina were a Christian married couple known to Augustine through their relative Ruferius. Augustine wrote to encourage them to fulfill their shared vow of continence and to treat the vow as a happy obligation to God.

nodes.name: Laetus
nodes.role: Christian layman and ascetic correspondent of Augustine
nodes.bio: Laetus was a Christian correspondent of Augustine who had entered the path of stricter discipleship but was being pulled back by family pressures. Augustine wrote urging him to carry his cross, serve the church, and provide rightly for household needs without abandoning his calling.

nodes.name: Marius Mercator
nodes.role: Latin Christian writer and anti-Pelagian polemicist
nodes.bio: Marius Mercator (born probably in North Africa around 390, died after 451) was a Latin Christian writer active against Pelagian teaching. Augustine's letter 193 praises his progress in defending Catholic doctrine and answers his questions about infant baptism, original sin, death, and the resurrection.

nodes.name: Hilarius, lay correspondent of Augustine
nodes.role: lay Christian correspondent from the Massilian controversy
nodes.bio: Hilarius was a lay Christian correspondent who reported to Augustine the objections circulating at Massilia and elsewhere in Gaul against Augustine's teaching on predestination, grace, perseverance, free choice, and the number of the elect.

nodes.name: Prosper of Aquitaine
nodes.role: Latin Christian writer and defender of Augustine's doctrine of grace
nodes.bio: Prosper of Aquitaine (c. 390-c. 455) was a Latin Christian writer from Gaul and one of Augustine's most important defenders in the controversy over grace and predestination. His letter to Augustine reports Massilian objections and asks for a clear answer.

nodes.name: Bishops of the Council of Zerta
nodes.bio: The bishops of the Council of Zerta were North African Catholic bishops, including Augustine among the signatories, who wrote in 412 after the Carthage conference to summarize the case against Donatist claims and call Donatist communities back to catholic unity.

nodes.name: Donatist communities
nodes.bio: The Donatist communities were North African Christians separated from the catholic communion over questions of persecution-era betrayal, church purity, rebaptism, and ecclesiastical legitimacy. Augustine and North African councils repeatedly addressed them after the 411 Carthage conference.

nodes.name: Castor, bishop of Perga
nodes.role: Bishop of Perga and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Castor was bishop of Perga in Pamphylia and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. In the surviving letter addressed to him, Severus intervenes in a dispute over the precedence of subdeacons, readers, and singers in Castor's church.

nodes.name: Stephen, bishop of Tripolis
nodes.role: Bishop of Tripolis and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Stephen was bishop of Tripolis and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. Severus answers him on whether a presbyter named Stephen could be enrolled among the clergy without a dismissal letter from the ordaining bishop.

nodes.name: Philoxenus, bishop of Doliche
nodes.role: Bishop of Doliche and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Philoxenus was bishop of Doliche and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. Severus writes to him about Romulus, a cleric seeking permission to lead prayers at Antioch while still under Philoxenus' inhibition.

nodes.name: Eucharius, bishop and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Bishop and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Eucharius was a bishop addressed by Severus of Antioch in a ruling about the proceedings against Firminus in the city of Paltus. His precise see is not stated in Brooks' heading, so the Paltus location is tied to the case discussed in the letter rather than to an independently verified see.

nodes.name: Cosmas, Polyeuctus, and Zeno, presbyters
nodes.role: Presbyters and correspondents of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Cosmas, Polyeuctus, and Zeno were presbyters addressed together by Severus of Antioch in a letter about judging a dispute only after both sides have had a chance to appear. Their exact city or church is not securely named in the Brooks heading.

nodes.name: Eustace, presbyter and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Presbyter and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Eustace was a presbyter who asked Severus of Antioch to ordain John as a deacon. Severus' answer turns on the canonical requirement that an enslaved man be manumitted before entering the clergy.

nodes.name: Julian, archimandrite of the monastery of Bassus
nodes.role: Archimandrite and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Julian was presbyter and archimandrite of the monastery of the blessed Bassus. During Severus' banishment he asked how the monastery could obtain priests and deacons in a time of persecution.

nodes.name: Archelaus, reader of Tyre
nodes.role: Reader of Tyre and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Archelaus was a reader of Tyre addressed by Severus of Antioch after readers there withdrew from communion with a repudiated bishop. Severus reassures him that an excommunication imposed for defending the orthodox faith had no force.

nodes.name: Master of the Offices addressed by Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Imperial Master of the Offices and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: This unnamed Master of the Offices was an imperial official addressed by Severus of Antioch during his episcopacy. The letter concerns the bishops of Second Syria, monastic disorder, and Severus' appeal for the official to report the truth to the emperor.

nodes.name: Musonius and Alexander, vindices of Anazarbus
nodes.role: Vindices of Anazarbus and correspondents of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Musonius and Alexander were vindices, civic legal officials, at Anazarbus. Severus writes to them about synodal unity, a repentant monk, and why the man should not return to Antioch.

nodes.name: John Canopites
nodes.role: Monastic father and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: John Canopites was a monastic father and correspondent of Severus of Antioch. Severus' letter praises his counsel, discusses communion discipline, and asks for his prayers during trial.

nodes.name: Simeon, archimandrite of the great monastery
nodes.role: Archimandrite and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Simeon was archimandrite of the great monastery and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. Severus urges him not to abandon governance of the monastic flock under the pretext of prayer and quietude.

nodes.name: Victor, bishop of Philadelphia
nodes.role: Bishop of Philadelphia and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Victor was bishop of Philadelphia and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. Severus asks him to send the monk John back to his monastery and commends Victor's obedience and love.

nodes.name: Stephen, bishop of Apamea
nodes.role: Bishop of Apamea and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Stephen was bishop of Apamea and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. Severus commends a man related to Marinus for possible clerical inclusion and warns Stephen not to ordain the monk John without his archimandrite's consent.

nodes.name: Wife of Calliopius the patrician
nodes.role: Aristocratic correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: The unnamed wife of Calliopius the patrician wrote to Severus of Antioch about a confession of faith. Severus answers on a diptych and encourages careful speech about Christ and the Trinity.

nodes.name: Aurelius the scholastic
nodes.role: Scholastic and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Aurelius was a scholastic addressed by Severus of Antioch about the clerical status of Thomas, whose body had been mutilated either by physicians because of illness or by his own act. The letter links Aurelius to Cassian's metropolis.

nodes.name: Timostratus, duke and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Duke and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Timostratus was a duke addressed by Severus of Antioch about petitions for ordination and the poverty of the church of Antioch. Severus explains why he cannot treat priestly ordination as a means of material support.

nodes.name: Cosmas, archimandrite of the monastery of Cyrus
nodes.role: Archimandrite and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Cosmas was archimandrite of the monastery of Cyrus and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. Severus answers him on the difference between an involuntary lapse committed in ignorance and voluntary communion with heretical teaching.

nodes.name: Simeon, archimandrite of the monastery at Teleda
nodes.role: Archimandrite and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Simeon was archimandrite of the monastery at Teleda and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. Severus urges him to receive people turning toward orthodox faith with patience and a spirit suited to healing.

nodes.name: Eustace, young monk and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Young monk and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Eustace was a young monk who wrote to Severus of Antioch about property he had left behind after entering the monastic life. Severus distinguishes renouncing possessions from litigating over them and advises a limited, lawful way to avoid later claims.

nodes.name: Monks of the monastery of Bassus addressed by Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Monastic correspondents of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: These monks of the monastery of Bassus were addressed by Severus of Antioch about a man who entered their monastery after leaving a wife and children. Severus tells them to clarify the facts and protect the public integrity of monastic discipline.

nodes.name: Stephen the reader, correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Reader and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Stephen was a church reader who asked Severus of Antioch about the public reading of praise-narratives for saints, especially material connected with Simeon. Severus' answer shows a reader helping shape what could be read in church.

nodes.name: Eutychian, governor of Apamea
nodes.role: Governor of Apamea and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Eutychian was governor of Apamea and a civil official addressed by Severus after reports that he had joined a feast led by a deprived bishop. Severus warns him that civil office does not make compromised communion safe.

nodes.name: Dioscorus, archbishop of Alexandria
nodes.role: Archbishop of Alexandria and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Dioscorus was archbishop of Alexandria and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. Severus writes to him during an embassy to the imperial capital, asking counsel about proposed terms of union with Cappadocian bishops.

nodes.name: Clergy and notables of Apamea addressed by Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Clergy and civic notables involved in the episcopal election at Apamea
nodes.bio: The clergy and notables of Apamea were addressed collectively by Severus during a disputed episcopal election. He urges them to act together and nominate three candidates known for orthodox faith, freedom from greed, virtue, and teaching ability.

nodes.name: Theodore, bishop of Olba
nodes.role: Bishop of Olba and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Theodore was bishop of Olba and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. He asked about a person whose baptism was uncertain, prompting Severus to recommend a conditional formula that avoided both neglect and rebaptism.

nodes.name: Theodore, tribune and notary
nodes.role: Tribune, notary, and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Theodore was a tribune and notary addressed by Severus before Severus' episcopate. He wanted the philosophic or monastic life, but Severus advises him to consider his wife, children, and household duties before withdrawing.

nodes.name: Conon the silentiary
nodes.role: Silentiary and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Conon was a silentiary, an imperial court official, who asked Severus for guidance about his daughter's marriage. Severus refuses to turn ascetic elders into private oracles and tells Conon to choose by faith and character.

nodes.name: Jannia, deaconess and archimandritess
nodes.role: Deaconess, archimandritess, and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Jannia was a deaconess and archimandritess responsible for a community of women. Severus answers a question brought by the deacon Theodore and advises her to combine strict governance with mercy, personal example, and gradual correction.

nodes.name: Hypatius, Master of the Soldiers
nodes.role: Master of the Soldiers and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Hypatius was a senior military official addressed by Severus about a church-property case involving Tarsus. Severus asks him not to let a civil appeal undo a judgment already handled by bishops and reputable legal experts.

nodes.name: John, count from Antaradus
nodes.role: Count from Antaradus and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: John was a count from Antaradus addressed by Severus about avoiding communion with those Severus regarded as holding contrary doctrine. The letter also mentions John's believing wife and a prelate of Area.

nodes.name: Monks of the monastery at Tagais addressed by Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Monastic community and correspondents of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: The monks of the monastery at Tagais were addressed by Severus after Neon reported that some were divided over names and reception rules. Severus urges them to keep the royal road of faith and avoid needless rebaptism or reanointing of converts.

nodes.name: Philip the presbyter, correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Presbyter and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Philip was a presbyter who wrote to Severus about sins confessed from youth and scruples over priestly ministry. Severus tells him to trust the testimony under which he was ordained and not bind himself beyond the church's judgment.

nodes.name: Unnamed woman advised on behalf of Maximus by Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Laywoman and correspondent advised in the name of Abba Maximus
nodes.bio: This unnamed woman asked, through Severus writing in Abba's name for brother Maximus, about continence, marriage, and life among virgins. The answer weighs ascetic desire against the obligations created by marriage and children.

nodes.name: Theodore, archimandrite of the monastery of Romanus
nodes.role: Presbyter, archimandrite, and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Theodore was a presbyter and archimandrite of the monastery of Romanus. Severus praises his ascetic life and answers his question about communion with exiled bishops and orthodox communities.

nodes.name: Clergy of Antaradus addressed by Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Collective clergy of Antaradus and correspondents of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: The clergy of Antaradus petitioned Severus about the need to nominate a shepherd and about property they said was being unjustly held from their church.

nodes.name: Ammian and Epagathus
nodes.role: Benefactors and correspondents of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Ammian and Epagathus were correspondents who spent money and effort on Severus' behalf during exile. Severus thanks them while also directing their gifts toward genuine clergy and orthodox discipline.

nodes.name: Archimandrite of the monastery of Simeon addressed by Severus
nodes.role: Archimandrite and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: This unnamed archimandrite of the monastery of Simeon corresponded with Severus about Nonnus, a cleric accused of contempt for ecclesiastical summonses and illicit gain.

nodes.name: Proclus and Eusebuna, bishops
nodes.role: Bishops and correspondents of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Proclus and Eusebuna were bishops addressed together by Severus about repentance, church communion, and the danger of treating association with doctrinal opponents as a small matter.

nodes.name: Georgia daughter of Anastasia the hypalissa
nodes.role: Laywoman and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Georgia, daughter of Anastasia the hypalissa, was a woman of high status whom Severus advised about salvation, family influence, and care for her father.

nodes.name: Zacharias of Pelusium
nodes.role: Correspondent of Severus of Antioch at Pelusium
nodes.bio: Zacharias of Pelusium asked Severus how to think about offerings and prayer when the giver remained in communion with people Severus judged unsound.

nodes.name: Ammonius, presbyter of Alexandria
nodes.role: Presbyter of Alexandria and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Ammonius was a presbyter of Alexandria who asked Severus about the commemoration of Peter Mongus and the treatment of inherited ecclesiastical memory.

nodes.name: Valeriana, deaconess and archimandritess
nodes.role: Deaconess, archimandritess, and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Valeriana was a deaconess and archimandritess placed over a community of sacred virgins. Severus writes to encourage strict but spiritually profitable governance.

nodes.name: Peter, bishop of Apamea
nodes.role: Bishop of Apamea and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Peter was bishop of Apamea and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. Severus answers his complaints about ordination, episcopal responsibility, and the limits of local clerical control.

nodes.name: Froclus, bishop and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Bishop and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Froclus was a bishop addressed by Severus during the years after expulsion. Brooks' OCR also makes the name look like Proclus, so the batch preserves the concordance form while noting the source difficulty.

nodes.name: Thecla the countess
nodes.role: Countess and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Thecla was a countess who wrote through the grammarian Stephen. Severus answers her by quoting prior advice on baptism, faith, and church discipline.

nodes.name: Theodore, Eastern Roman monk and correspondent of Severus
nodes.role: Monk and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: This Theodore was a monk described by Brooks as connected by marriage to imperial prefects. Severus addressed him about a disputed entry into monastic life and the claims of family obligations after a vow.

nodes.name: Nonnus, bishop of Seleucia in Syria
nodes.role: Bishop of Seleucia and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Nonnus was bishop of Seleucia in Syria. Severus rebuked him for failing to settle a monastery discipline case involving Pelagius and for leaving the burden to Severus and the count of the East.

nodes.name: Isidora, correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Laywoman or ascetic correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Isidora wrote to Severus about grief, family bonds, burial, and religious practice. Severus' answer treats her endurance as an offering shaped by hope in the resurrection.

nodes.name: John, Philoxenus, and Thomas, confessing bishops on the hill of Marde
nodes.role: Bishops and correspondents of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: John, Philoxenus, and Thomas were bishops living as confessors on the hill of Marde. Severus compares their exile and pastoral work to Elijah at Horeb and advises them on receiving people baptized by doctrinal opponents.

nodes.name: Archimandrite of the monastery of Bassus addressed by Severus
nodes.role: Archimandrite and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: This unnamed archimandrite of the monastery of Bassus wrote to Severus after the death of Cosmas of Apamea. Severus answers a difficult request about Cosmas' legacy, communion, and the handling of those caught in error.

nodes.name: Alypius, correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Lay aristocrat and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Alypius was a person of rank who consulted Severus on marriage, suspicion, and separation from his wife. Severus answers with gospel and Pauline rules about marriage, evidence, and mercy in doubtful cases.

nodes.name: John the tribune, correspondent in the name of Leontius
nodes.role: Tribune and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: John the tribune wrote in the name of Leontius before Severus' episcopate. Severus answers his criticism of Timothy of Alexandria and discusses how pastoral decisions may change while preserving the same aim of salvation.

nodes.name: Constantine, bishop and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Bishop and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Constantine was a bishop who corresponded with Severus before or around the years of Severus' patriarchate. In Brooks letter I.1, Severus reports his discussion in the capital about the formula of satisfaction sent to Flavian of Antioch, and he urges Constantine and his circle to stand firm in the orthodox confession.

nodes.name: Photius and Andrew, archimandrites in Caria
nodes.role: Archimandrites and correspondents of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Photius and Andrew were archimandrites of monasteries in Caria. Severus praises their ascetic discipline and answers a disciplinary question about receiving someone ordained by doctrinal opponents, the error of re-anointing, and the purpose of canonical restrictions around communion.

nodes.name: John scholastic of Bostra
nodes.role: Scholastic and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: John was a scholastic associated with Bostra who sent Severus difficult canonical questions. In Brooks letter VIII.4, Severus answers him on the force of anathema and on a self-mutilated monk who had later been ordained, distinguishing repentance and salvation from eligibility for clerical office.

nodes.name: John, bishop of Alexandria Minor
nodes.role: Bishop of Alexandria Minor and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: John was bishop of Alexandria Minor in Cilicia Secunda. Severus wrote to him after subdeacons of his church complained that their traditional freedom from weekly service in the bishop's house had been disturbed.

nodes.name: Unnamed correspondent on reception of converts from Diphysitism
nodes.role: Correspondent of Severus of Antioch on the reception of converts
nodes.bio: This unnamed correspondent asked Severus of Antioch whether converts from the two-nature party should be received by baptism, chrism, or ordination. Severus answered in Select Letters V.6 with a long canonical argument from earlier bishops, councils, and pastoral precedents.

nodes.name: Clergy of Apamea addressed by Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: The clergy of the metropolis of Apamea were addressed collectively by Severus of Antioch after the death of their bishop Isaac. Severus urges them to choose episcopal candidates by canonical judgment rather than worldly pressure and orders the restoration of the church steward who had been displaced while Isaac was dying.

nodes.name: Eusebius, deacon of Apamea and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Eusebius was a deacon at Apamea addressed by Severus of Antioch in a short disciplinary letter about Libanius, a presbyter accused of demanding interest on a loan. Severus asks Eusebius to work through the church stewards and archdeacon so the matter can be corrected before canonical penalties become necessary.

nodes.name: Philoxenus, bishop of Hierapolis
nodes.role: Bishop of Hierapolis and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Philoxenus was bishop of Hierapolis, also known as Mabbug, and a correspondent of Severus of Antioch. In this letter Severus asks his judgment about clergy who had bought ordination from Flavian and were now seeking forgiveness through court patrons, monastic leaders, and other bishops.

nodes.name: Sergius of Cyrrhus and Marion of Sura
nodes.role: Joint episcopal recipients of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Sergius, bishop of Cyrrhus, and Marion, bishop of Sura, were addressed jointly by Severus of Antioch in a long letter on receiving repentant clergy and people baptized by doctrinal opponents. Because the letter has two episcopal recipients in different cities, the corpus keeps the combined recipient without assigning a single destination coordinate.

nodes.name: Cassian, Constantine, Antoninus, and other Syrian bishops at Alexandria
nodes.role: Exiled Syrian bishops under the Antiochene see
nodes.bio: Cassian, Constantine, Antoninus, and other bishops from Syria were followers of the Antiochene see who had taken refuge in Alexandria during Severus of Antioch's exile. Severus addresses them collectively in Select Letters I.53, praising their handling of the cases of Paul of Olba and Elpidius and urging a canonical but merciful policy toward deposed bishops and repentant Christians.

nodes.name: Conon the brigand-chaser and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Imperial security official and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Conon, described by Brooks as a brigand-chaser, was an imperial official addressed by Severus of Antioch during Severus' episcopate. In Select Letters I.45, Severus urges Conon to support church discipline after a woman improperly claimed the rank of deaconess and was stripped of that supposed office.

nodes.name: Anatolius, correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus
nodes.bio: Anatolius is the named recipient of Evagrius Ponticus, Letter 25, in the CPG 2437 parallel edition. Evagrius addresses him as an ascetic whose thoughts and prayer need careful testing.

nodes.name: Deaconess Severa
nodes.bio: Severa was a deaconess and ascetic correspondent in Evagrius Ponticus's network. The CPG 2437 parallel edition labels Letter 20 as addressed to her.

nodes.name: Eustathius, correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus
nodes.bio: Eustathius is the named recipient of Evagrius Ponticus, Letter 21, in the CPG 2437 parallel edition. The letter consoles him after the loss of a shared spiritual father.

nodes.name: Rufinus of Aquileia and Melania the Elder
nodes.bio: Rufinus of Aquileia and Melania the Elder are grouped as joint recipients of Evagrius Ponticus, Letter 32, in the CPG 2437 parallel edition. Both belonged to the ascetic network centered around the Mount of Olives.

nodes.name: Unknown ascetic correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus
nodes.bio: Unknown ascetic correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus is the working identity for Letter 15 in the Evagrius CPG 2437 parallel tradition. The source preserves the correspondence context but not enough evidence for a secure personal identity or destination geolocation.

nodes.name: Cecropius, correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus
nodes.bio: Cecropius is named in the vocative in Evagrius Ponticus, Letter 59. Evagrius consoles him over physical distance and teaches that virtue, not place, joins people to the saints.

nodes.name: Hymettius, correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus
nodes.bio: Hymettius is named in the vocative in Evagrius Ponticus, Letter 58. The letter discusses promises, withdrawal to the cell, grief, contemplation, and the knowledge of the Holy Trinity.

nodes.name: Theophorus, correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus
nodes.bio: Theophorus is a working recipient identity for Evagrius Ponticus, Letter 48, based on the source's vocative address. The name may function as an honorific meaning God-bearing rather than as a secure personal name.
