nodes.name: Unknown priest, correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus
nodes.bio: This unnamed priest is the working identity for Evagrius Ponticus, Letter 47. The letter speaks of the recipient's priestly gift and asks him to feed others with the knowledge of God.

nodes.name: Unknown wavering correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus
nodes.bio: Unknown wavering correspondent of Evagrius Ponticus is the working identity for Letter 54 in the Evagrius CPG 2437 parallel tradition. The source preserves the correspondence context but not enough evidence for a secure personal identity or destination geolocation.

nodes.name: Unnamed brothers, correspondents of Evagrius Ponticus
nodes.bio: These unnamed brothers are grouped recipients in Evagrius Ponticus, Letter 60. The letter teaches about love, anger, detachment from the world, and the knowledge of God.

nodes.name: Unknown recipient of Severus of Antioch I.54
nodes.bio: The recipient of Select Letters I.54 is not preserved in Brooks' table of contents or OCR heading. The surviving body of the letter speaks of news from the East, the orthodox in Antioch, and Eustochius, a deacon of the church in Alexandria.

nodes.name: Anastasius the count, son of Sergius
nodes.role: Count and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Anastasius, identified by Brooks as a count and son of Sergius, was a lay aristocratic correspondent of Severus of Antioch. In Select Letters III.1, Severus sends him the communion or oblation he requested and emphasizes that shared faith, not the personal rank of the minister, gives the gift its value.

nodes.name: Eleusinius, bishop and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Bishop and correspondent of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: Eleusinius was a bishop addressed by Severus of Antioch in Select Letters VI.1. Severus writes to him with unusually personal warmth, then turns to news about trials, clerical politics, the new bishop in Constantinople, and rumors about an anathema against Severus.

nodes.name: Peter, bishop of Trecala
nodes.role: bishop of Trecala/Triocala and visitor of the church of Agrigentum
nodes.bio: Peter was bishop of Trecala, usually identified with ancient Triocala in Sicily, and a correspondent of Pope Gregory the Great. In Gregory, Register V.12, he is charged with visiting the church of Agrigentum and is assigned the bishop's quarter of that church's income while he carries the responsibility.

nodes.name: Felix, subdeacon and rector of the Appian patrimony
nodes.role: subdeacon and manager of the Appian patrimony
nodes.bio: Felix was a subdeacon and rector of the Appian patrimony, a manager of church estates near Rome. Gregory, Register XIV.14, orders him to remove the Aquae Salviae estate and related lands from his registers and hand them over to Saint Paul's church for the upkeep of its lamps.

nodes.name: Patricians addressed by Severus of Antioch
nodes.role: Roman aristocratic recipients of Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: The patricians addressed in Select Letters II.1 were high-ranking Roman aristocrats whom Severus asked to convey his defense to the emperor. The letter responds to accusations that Severus and his associates officiated without priestly rank or re-ordained clergy, and it frames the answer as a formal appeal to powerful lay intermediaries.

nodes.name: Orthodox Christians at Emesa
nodes.role: Christian community addressed by Severus of Antioch
nodes.bio: The orthodox Christians at Emesa received Severus' long warning against the fraudulent episcopal claims of Gregory and Isaiah. In Select Letters II.3, Severus treats Emesa as a tested and loyal community that should refuse communion or recognition to irregular claimants who undermine canonical episcopal order.

nodes.name: Magnus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.role: official or athletic patronage correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Magnus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 843, where Libanius asks him to help recruit athletes from Egypt for the games at Daphne. The letter implies influence in Egyptian athletic or official circles, but it does not by itself prove a precise location.

nodes.name: Ursus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Ursus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 859, dated 388. Libanius praises his judgment, reputation, and thoughtful letters, then asks him to help Diognetus.

nodes.name: Diogenes, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Diogenes is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 860, dated 388. Libanius sends Diognetus to him with a letter of recommendation. The import uses a Libanius-specific scaffold to avoid conflating him with other correspondents named Diogenes.

nodes.name: Eutychianus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Eutychianus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 864, dated 388. Libanius appeals to his generosity for a poor woman and leaves the civic embassy in his hands.

nodes.name: Rufinus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Rufinus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 865, dated 388. The letter concerns a delayed reply, bilingual translation of Libanius' earlier letter, and help for Antiochene ambassadors.

nodes.name: Promotus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Promotus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 867, dated 388. Libanius asks him for a first-hand account of the current war, calling it a general's gift to an orator.

nodes.name: Antiochianus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Antiochianus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 869, dated 388. Libanius advises him to stop showing Libanius' speeches to hostile critics in order to avoid literary quarrels.

nodes.name: Petrus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Petrus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 880, dated 388. Libanius sends Eusebius to him and warns Petrus not to create enemies by praising Libanius too freely.

nodes.name: Antherius, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Antherius is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 881, dated 388. Libanius asks him to intervene for Gaianus against unfair treatment.

nodes.name: Eupsychius, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Eupsychius is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 888, dated 388. Libanius asks him to prevent a doctor from displacing an existing suitor and damaging an agreed marriage.

nodes.name: Brasidas, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.role: friend and patronage correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Brasidas is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 889, dated 388. Libanius presses him to help his kinsman Romulus and proposes a property settlement at Daphne.

nodes.name: Gessius, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.role: teacher and former student of Libanius
nodes.bio: Gessius is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 891, dated 388. Libanius praises his letters from Egypt and urges him to marry so that his children might later be educated in Antioch.

nodes.name: Aristaenetus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Aristaenetus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 895, dated 388. Libanius apologizes for a long silence, prays for his health, and discusses Polybius and Leontius.

nodes.name: Heraclitus, correspondent of Libanius
nodes.bio: Heraclitus is addressed by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 899, dated 388. Libanius praises the truthfulness of his letter and discusses Palladius, Lucianus, and hopes for help in Phoenicia.

nodes.name: Envoys, correspondents of Libanius
nodes.bio: These envoys are addressed collectively by Libanius in Foerster Epistle 890, dated 388, in a short appeal concerning Romulus.
